clinicalPearls: Persistent difficult, infrequent or incomplete defecation not attributable to a structural, metabolic or drug cause and not meeting criteria for irritable bowel syndrome
Features include straining, hard or lumpy stools, a sense of incomplete evacuation and use of manual manoeuvres
It differs from constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome mainly by the absence of predominant abdominal pain
Broad mechanisms include normal-transit, slow-transit and evacuation (defecatory) disorders, which guide treatment
Secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, medications and colorectal obstruction must be excluded
Management uses fibre and fluid, osmotic and stimulant laxatives, and newer secretagogues or prokinetics for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Functional constipation encompasses several mechanisms of impaired stool passage in the absence of an identifiable organic cause. Normal-transit constipation reflects perceived difficulty despite normal colonic transit, slow-transit constipation results from reduced colonic propulsive activity, and defecatory disorders arise from impaired coordination of the pelvic floor and anal sphincter during evacuation. Disordered neuromuscular control of the colon and anorectum, sometimes with altered fluid handling, underlies the symptoms, and overlap between mechanisms is common.
additionalInvestigations: History and examination including rectal examination for evacuation disorder
Bloods to exclude metabolic causes such as thyroid dysfunction and hypercalcaemia
Colonic transit studies where slow transit is suspected
Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion for suspected defecatory disorder
Colonoscopy where alarm features or obstruction are suspected
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, anaemia or weight loss
New or rapidly progressive constipation in an older patient
Neurological signs suggesting a secondary cause
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic but benign, and most patients respond to a stepwise regimen, with defecatory disorders often improving specifically with pelvic floor retraining.
pitfalls: Failing to identify a coexisting defecatory disorder that will not respond to laxatives alone
Overlooking secondary metabolic or drug causes
Relying on stimulant laxatives without addressing the underlying mechanism
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: First-line lifestyle measures with increased dietary fibre, adequate fluid intake and physical activity
Osmotic laxatives such as macrogol as the mainstay of pharmacotherapy
Stimulant laxatives added when the response is inadequate
Secretagogues such as linaclotide, or the prokinetic prucalopride, for refractory or slow-transit disease
Pelvic floor biofeedback and retraining for defecatory (evacuation) disorders
Review and withdraw constipating medications and exclude secondary causes such as hypothyroidism and hypercalcaemia
Escalate to specialist anorectal investigation when disease is refractory or alarm features emerge
